reader.title: Attempted lynching of Bright Picket
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob attacked a jail 'with the object of lynching a prisoner', and the sheriff repelled it, an attempted lynching (A1).

A mob of one hundred masked men tried to lynch the prisoner, but the sheriff fought them off and no one is reported killed, so this was an attempt, not a completed lynching (A1). No accusation against the prisoner is stated.
Only one brief, in a Baton Rouge paper, reports the attack; no second report was found (A1).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Bright Picket was an attack by a mob of one hundred masked men on a jail in Texas, reported in early December 1881, with the object of lynching Picket, a prisoner held there.
The sheriff, Hopkins, assisted by his wife, fought the mob off, and no one is reported killed.
The episode is known from a single brief that credited the sheriff and his wife with the defense.
The surviving account says nothing about why Picket was in jail or what charge, if any, he faced.
It names neither the town nor the county, and it does not give the race of the prisoner or of the men who came for him.
According to the brief, one hundred masked men attacked the jail intending to lynch Picket.
Sheriff Hopkins resisted them with his wife's help and drove them off, so the prisoner was not taken from the jail.
No deaths, injuries or damage to the building are mentioned, and the time of the attack is not given.
No report of arrests among the mob, of an investigation, or of what became of Picket appears in the coverage.
The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge carried the story on December 3, 1881, as a one-sentence item without a headline.
Its wording centered on the sheriff, who "fought off a mob of one hundred masked men," and on his wife's part in the defense, while offering no comment on the mob or on the prisoner.
No other newspaper version of the attack, and no report from a Texas paper, appears in the coverage.
